title: Language core: exceptions, context managers and generators (Python)
seriesTitle: Python: exceptions, context managers and generators
seriesDescription: try/except/finally, context managers, comprehensions, generators, itertools, functools. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: try/except/else/finally, exception hierarchy and chaining, context managers, comprehensions, generators and lazy iteration, plus the usual finally and default-argument traps.
source: Python docs: built-in exceptions and hierarchy, errors and exceptions tutorial, contextlib, itertools, generators; Real Python; Fluent Python (Ramalho); GeeksforGeeks and Toptal Python interview lists

questions.prompt: Write a Python context manager function opened(path) that opens a text file, yields it, and always closes it, so it can be used as: with opened("a.txt") as f: ...  (write the function only).
questions.explanation: A class defining __enter__ and __exit__ is equivalent. Putting yield inside with open(path) as f: also closes the file. Without try/finally an exception in the with-body would skip the cleanup after yield.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?
def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        print("finally", end=" ")
print(f())
What is the output?

options.text: try (then finally)
options.why: finally runs before the function actually hands control back, so it prints first.

options.text: finally try
options.why: Correct: finally prints during the return, then print outputs the returned value.

options.text: try
options.why: The finally clause always runs on the way out, so something else is printed too.

options.text: finally
options.why: The returned string "try" is still printed by the outer print call.

questions.explanation: try/except/else/finally: else runs only if no exception was raised, finally always runs. (Verified by running it.)

questions.text: In Python, the {1} clause of a try statement runs only when no exception occurred, and the {2} clause always runs; to re-raise with the original as the cause, write raise NewError from {3}.
questions.explanation: else keeps the guarded region small so that only the risky call is covered by except. raise X from e sets __cause__; raise X from None suppresses the chain display.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python print?
g = (x * x for x in range(3))
print(list(g), list(g), sum(g))
What is the output?

options.why: That would be true for a list, not a generator; the iterator is consumed by the first list(g).
sum(g) also sees an exhausted generator.
Correct: the first list drains the generator, so the second list and the sum see nothing.

options.text: TypeError: generator is exhausted
options.why: Python does not raise here; an exhausted generator simply yields nothing more.

questions.explanation: Generators are one-shot iterators. If you need two passes, build a list, tee with itertools.tee, or recreate the generator. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Write a Python generator function chunks(seq, n) that yields successive slices of length n from the sequence (the last one may be shorter).

checks.label: steps through with range or a loop

questions.explanation: itertools.batched(it, n) does this in Python 3.12+. A generator keeps memory flat because it produces one chunk at a time.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Calling a Python generator function runs none of its body until the first next() call.
questions.reason: A generator function computes all of its values into a list when it is called.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the call just creates a generator object); R is false, since values are produced lazily one at a time.

questions.explanation: That laziness lets generators model infinite sequences and stream large files without loading them into memory.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Python 3, the loop variable of a list comprehension remains visible in the enclosing scope after the comprehension ends.
questions.reason: In Python 2, list comprehension variables leaked into the enclosing scope.

whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: Python 3 gives comprehensions their own scope (A is false); R is true for Python 2.

questions.explanation: A for loop statement still leaks its variable; only comprehensions and generator expressions have their own scope.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about the Python exception hierarchy.

options.text: A bare except: clause also catches KeyboardInterrupt.
options.why: Correct: bare except catches BaseException, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit.

options.text: except Exception: catches KeyboardInterrupt.
options.why: Wrong: KeyboardInterrupt derives from BaseException, not Exception, so it passes through.

options.text: KeyError is a subclass of LookupError.
options.why: Correct: KeyError and IndexError both derive from LookupError.

options.text: except Exception: catches SystemExit raised by sys.exit().
options.why: Wrong: SystemExit derives from BaseException, which is why sys.exit() is not swallowed by except Exception.

options.text: FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError.
options.why: Correct: since Python 3.3 IOError is an alias of OSError and FileNotFoundError is one of its subclasses.

questions.explanation: Catch the narrowest exception you can; at most except Exception at a top-level boundary. Verified with issubclass checks.

questions.prompt: Match each Python feature to what it does.

right.text: Calls __enter__ on entry and __exit__ even when the body fails
Runs only when the try body raised nothing
Always runs, whether or not an exception occurred
Re-raises the exception currently being handled
Turns the exception into a warning

questions.explanation: Know which clause runs when: else on success only, finally always, bare raise to propagate unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does sum(n * n for n in range(1, 7) if n % 2 == 0) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, whose squares are 4 + 16 + 36 = 56.

questions.prompt: What does len([v * 2 for sub in [[1, 2], [3], []] for v in sub if v * 2 > 2]) return?
questions.explanation: The doubled values are 2, 4 and 6; only 4 and 6 are greater than 2, so the list has 2 elements.

questions.prompt:
Consider:

def f():
    x = 1
    try:
        return x
    finally:
        x = 2

What does f() return?
questions.explanation: The return value is evaluated before finally runs, so rebinding x afterwards does not change it.

questions.prompt: Given a list of strings words, write Python that builds a dict by_length mapping each length to the list of words with that length.
questions.model:
from collections import defaultdict
by_length = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    by_length[len(w)].append(w)
questions.explanation: setdefault(len(w), []).append(w) and itertools.groupby over a sorted list also work.

questions.prompt:
What happens when this Python code runs?

def f():
    try:
        raise RuntimeError("x")
    finally:
        return 7

print(f())

What is the outcome?

options.text: It prints 7 and the RuntimeError is discarded
options.why: Correct: a return inside finally replaces the propagating exception.

options.text: It raises RuntimeError: x after finally runs
options.why: The return in finally cancels the exception, so it never propagates.

options.text: It prints None because the try body failed
options.why: The finally block returns 7 explicitly.

options.text: SyntaxError: return is not allowed in finally
options.why: It is legal (though discouraged and flagged by linters).

questions.explanation: Never return, break or continue inside finally: it silently swallows exceptions.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Python, d.get(key, expensive()) calls expensive() even when key is present in d.
questions.reason: Python evaluates call arguments before the call is made.

whys.a: Correct: the default argument is computed before get runs, so it is always evaluated.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: the default argument is computed before get runs, so it is always evaluated.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: the default argument is computed before get runs, so it is always evaluated.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: the default argument is computed before get runs, so it is always evaluated.

questions.explanation: Use an if/else or a conditional expression to compute the default only when needed.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In "with a() as x, b() as y:" the context manager b is exited before a.
questions.reason: A context manager must define __enter__ and __exit__ methods.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: Both statements are true, but the exit order follows nesting (last entered, first exited), not the protocol methods.
whys.b: Correct: Both statements are true, but the exit order follows nesting (last entered, first exited), not the protocol methods.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: Both statements are true, but the exit order follows nesting (last entered, first exited), not the protocol methods.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: Both statements are true, but the exit order follows nesting (last entered, first exited), not the protocol methods.

questions.explanation: Multiple context managers behave like nested with statements, so they unwind in reverse order.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

m = map(print, [1, 2])
print("x")

What is printed?

options.text: Only x, because nothing consumed the lazy map
options.why: Correct: map returns an iterator; print is not called on the items until you iterate.

options.text: 1, 2 and then x, because map runs eagerly
options.why: That would need map to run eagerly as it did in Python 2.

options.text: x, then 1 and 2, printed when the program exits
options.why: Nothing iterates the map object, so the items are never printed.

options.text: A TypeError, because print returns None and cannot be mapped
options.why: map does not care about the return values until it is consumed.

questions.explanation: Wrap map in list() or loop over it to force evaluation; do not use map for side effects.

options.text: {1: 'a', 2: 'cc'}, since a later duplicate key overwrites
options.why: Correct: the second value for key 2 replaces the first.

options.text: {1: 'a', 2: 'bb'}, since the first value wins
options.why: Dict assignment always overwrites, so the last value wins.

options.text: A ValueError for the duplicate key 2
options.why: Dict comprehensions allow repeated keys.

options.text: {1: ['a'], 2: ['bb', 'cc']}, grouped automatically
options.why: Nothing groups values; each key keeps a single value.

questions.explanation: Unlike a collector that rejects duplicates, a dict comprehension silently keeps the last value.
